newsitem.title: USA: Barge capsizes with 12,500 tons of urea in Alaska.
newsitem.headline: Barge capsizes with 12,500 tons of urea in Alaska.

text.p: A barge that capsized with 12,500 tons of chemical fertilizer aboard may still hold much of its cargo, officials said on Wednesday, citing reports from divers examining the disabled vessel.

Divers said the hatches remained closed on the barge that capsized over the weekend in Alaska's Cook Inlet with a cargo of urea fertilizer. The barge collided with the tug that was towing it from the Unocal plant that produced the urea.
Terry Anderson, a spokesman for Crowley Marine Services, the operator of the barge and tug, said the exact quantity of cargo lost was unknown.

The barge was towed to Kachemak Bay, offshore from Homer, a fishing and tourism center at the southern tip of Kenai Peninsula. But the vessel may be towed out of Kachemak Bay if significant quantities of fertilizer remain in its holds.
"Kachemak Bay is a critical habitat area, and they don't want that in the bay," Anderson said.
Unocal said urea was unlikely to pose any health risks because it was produced naturally by the human body.
Denise Newbould, environmental supervisor for Unocal's fertilizer plant at Nikiski, north of Homer, said urea does not accumulate and is not considered a toxin or carcinogen.
Human urine is 80 percent urea, she said.
Tests also show the urea fertilizer, which is formed into small pellets and produced with methane and ammonia, dissolves and disperses rapidly in the water column, Newbould said.
"If you take the worst-case scenario, it's a lot of product, but the receiving water body is so great and it dissolves so quickly," she said.
